idiom_name: WeakReference<T>.TryGetTarget + ConditionalWeakTable<TKey,TValue> (short vs long weak references)
implementation_notes: .NET provides weak references in the base class library: WeakReference<T> is the typed form (the non-generic WeakReference predates generics), TryGetTarget performs the promotion and returns false once the target has been reclaimed, and the constructor flag selects short weak references (target nulled at collection) versus long ones (retained after Finalize has run, with a state the framework calls unpredictable). For data attached to an object by identity, ConditionalWeakTable<TKey,TValue> is the weak-key table: it does not keep keys alive and removes an entry as soon as no references to the key exist outside the table, which is how compilers attach fields at run time and why it is the right shape for side tables. For event handlers the framework's answer to the same leak is the weak event manager (WeakEventManager) rather than a weak delegate.
pitfalls: TryGetTarget guarantees the target only for the duration of the call: keep the out value in a local for the whole operation, or another thread's last reference can still drop it.

Short versus long weak references: long weak references (constructor flag true, and ConditionalWeakTable entries) can see an object whose finalizer has already run and whose state is documented as unpredictable - never touch the target from a finalizer path.
ConditionalWeakTable keys are compared by reference identity, and a value that references its own key keeps the pair alive - attach only data that does not point back at the key.
ConditionalWeakTable is not enumerable and exposes no Count, so a structure that needs to know what remains must keep its own bookkeeping.
